blocks.content: The TCP overview topic mentioned the three way handshake briefly, just enough to know it exists before any real data can flow. This topic gives you the full mechanics: exactly what each of the three steps does, why it takes exactly three and not two or four, and what happens when something goes wrong along the way.

Before two devices can reliably exchange data over TCP, they need to agree on a few things first: that both sides are actually reachable and listening, and critically, what starting sequence number each side will use for its own data. The sequence numbering itself is covered in full in its own dedicated topic later in this module. Here, you will see exactly how that starting agreement gets made.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014213702-873761909.png
blocks.alt: The three way handshake at a glance: SYN, SYN ACK, ACK, before any real data flows

blocks.content: 1. Step One: SYN

The client that wants to open a connection sends a segment with the SYN flag set, along with a randomly chosen initial sequence number it will use for its own data going forward. This single segment says two things at once: I want to connect, and here is exactly where my sequence numbering will start.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014216131-359661214.png
blocks.alt: Step one: the client sends SYN, proposing its own starting sequence number

blocks.title: Why the number matters right away
blocks.content: Every byte the client sends after this point will be numbered starting from this exact value. Getting this number agreed on up front is what makes the sequence number tracking covered later in this module actually work correctly from the very first byte.
2. Step Two: SYN ACK

The server responds with its own SYN, containing its own independently chosen random initial sequence number, combined with an ACK acknowledging the client sequence number. This single segment genuinely does two separate jobs at once: agreeing to the connection and proposing its own starting point, AND confirming it received the client opening message.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014218193-133850888.png
blocks.alt: Step two: the server responds with SYN ACK, doing two jobs in one segment

blocks.content: 3. Step Three: ACK

The client sends a final acknowledgment, confirming the server sequence number. At this exact point, both sides have independently confirmed they can hear each other, and the connection is now officially established. Real application data can start flowing immediately after this.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014220202-742537230.png
blocks.alt: Step three: the client sends the final ACK, and the connection is now fully established

blocks.content: 4. A Full Worked Example With Real Numbers
blocks.text: 4. A Full Worked Example With Real Numbers

blocks.content: Tracing through concrete numbers makes this click. Say the client picks initial sequence number 1000, and the server independently picks initial sequence number 5000. The client sends SYN with sequence 1000. The server responds with SYN ACK, its own sequence 5000, and acknowledgment 1001, meaning it correctly received the client starting point and is now expecting the next byte after it. The client then sends ACK with acknowledgment 5001, confirming the server starting point the same way.

{"headers":["Step","Segment","What it carries"],"rows":[["1","SYN","Client proposes sequence 1000"],["2","SYN ACK","Server proposes sequence 5000, acknowledges 1001"],["3","ACK","Client acknowledges 5001"]]}
5. Why Exactly Three Steps, Not Two, Not Four
blocks.text: 5. Why Exactly Three Steps, Not Two, Not Four

blocks.content: Two steps genuinely is not enough. If the client sent SYN and the server just started sending data with no ACK back at all, the client could never be sure the server actually received its SYN correctly in the first place. Only one direction would have been confirmed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014221936-394513008.png
blocks.alt: Two steps only confirms one direction; three steps lets both sides independently confirm they can send and receive

blocks.content: Three steps is the genuine minimum needed for BOTH sides to independently prove, to themselves and to each other, that they can both send and receive successfully. A fourth step would be redundant, since by the end of step three, both sides already have everything they need to know the connection works in both directions.
6. Why the Initial Numbers Are Randomized
blocks.text: 6. Why the Initial Numbers Are Randomized

blocks.content: If initial sequence numbers always started at some predictable, fixed value, an attacker watching or guessing at a connection could more easily predict what numbers are coming next, and potentially inject or hijack traffic into an ongoing connection. Starting from a genuinely random number for every single new connection makes this meaningfully harder to pull off.

blocks.title: A real security consideration, not just theory
blocks.content: This randomization is a genuine, deliberate security measure, not an arbitrary implementation detail. Predictable sequence numbers were a real, exploited weakness in early networking history, which is exactly why modern systems randomize them carefully.
7. The Connection States Along the Way
blocks.text: 7. The Connection States Along the Way

blocks.content: A TCP socket genuinely moves through a sequence of named states during this process, and this state tracking is real, not just a conceptual convenience, it is part of why establishing a TCP connection carries genuine overhead on both ends.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014224495-587488687.png
blocks.alt: The connection states a socket moves through during the handshake, from CLOSED to fully ESTABLISHED

8. What Happens If a SYN Gets Lost
blocks.text: 8. What Happens If a SYN Gets Lost

blocks.content: If the initial SYN, or the SYN ACK response, gets lost somewhere along the way, the sending side simply times out waiting for the expected response and automatically resends it. This is exactly why establishing a new TCP connection can occasionally feel slightly slow on a flaky or congested network, the handshake itself is being retried under the hood.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014226174-161074621.png
blocks.alt: If a SYN or SYN ACK is lost, the sender times out and automatically resends it

blocks.content: 9. The Real Cost of This Setup
blocks.text: 9. The Real Cost of This Setup

blocks.content: Picking up a phone and calling someone captures this well. You dial, hello is echoed back, can you hear me, and you confirm yes I can hear you, only after this brief exchange does the actual conversation begin. That brief back and forth is the three way handshake in miniature.

This entire exchange has to complete before a single byte of real application data is sent, and this is exactly the setup cost UDP deliberately skips entirely. If the round trip time between two points is 100 milliseconds, the handshake alone costs roughly one and a half round trips, about 150 milliseconds, spent purely on setup before the very first real byte has moved at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014227850-30917134.png
blocks.alt: On a connection with 100ms round trip time, the handshake alone costs about 150ms before any real data moves
